strengths: The paper addresses a difficult and relevant computer-vision problem: reconstructing fast, translucent, emissive flames using only three commodity cameras. The combination of synchronized high-speed capture, explicit static/dynamic decomposition, and Gaussian rendering is practically appealing.

The proposed pipeline is coherent: stereo and monocular depth stabilize the static background, while multi-view optical flow supplies a useful initialization for a FreeTimeGS-style dynamic representation. Explicit Gaussian lifetimes and velocities also provide an interpretable motion representation.

The captured dataset is reasonably diverse, covering 17 scenes with several fuels, flame scales, backgrounds, wind conditions, and smoke levels. Per-scene results, runtime information, and several ablations are included in the supplement.

The reported flame-region improvements over two 4DGS baselines are substantial, and the qualitative examples show sharper flame appearance and much less degenerate rendered depth. Separately pretraining the static scene is convincingly supported by the JointOpt ablation.
The paper is generally clear, visually polished, and candid about limitations involving optical flow, linear motion, smoke, and foreground/background interaction.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General, although it also has substantial Applied/Systems and Dataset/Benchmark aspects. Under the default type, the algorithmic novelty is modest: the representation is explicitly FreeTimeGS-based, while most of the contribution is an integration of existing 3DGS, stereo, monocular depth, optical flow, and synchronization components.

The central novel-view reconstruction claim is not adequately evaluated. Every eighth temporal frame is held out, apparently from the same three cameras used for training; this tests temporal interpolation at known viewpoints rather than unseen-view synthesis. Novel camera trajectories are shown only without ground truth, so the claimed 3D generalization cannot be quantitatively verified.

The depth evaluation is circular and not a reliable measure of geometric accuracy. RMSE is computed against an aligned Depth Anything V2 prediction, while aligned predictions from that same model directly regularize the proposed reconstruction. The baselines do not receive this supervision, and monocular depth is especially unreliable for transparent flames. Consequently, the very large reported depth advantage cannot establish accurate fire geometry.

The derivation of the 3D flow constraint is questionable. Equation 6 imposes only the scalar condition (F-u_i)^T u_i=0. Matching a 2D optical-flow vector under perspective projection generally requires two constraints through the projection Jacobian, J_i(x)F=f_i. The stated condition does not constrain image-plane motion orthogonal to u_i and therefore does not, in general, guarantee the claimed reprojection consistency. This needs derivation or validation.

The baseline study does not isolate the proposed innovations fairly. It omits a direct FreeTimeGS baseline and configurations that give competing dynamic methods the same static-scene decomposition, depth initialization, or regularization. Thus, improvements may primarily result from strong scene-specific priors and separate background reconstruction rather than the proposed 3D-flow initialization.

Evidence for several highlighted components is weak. Removing rolling-shutter rendering is essentially neutral and is slightly better on some aggregate metrics. A deliberately introduced one-frame desynchronization produces only a small reduction. Random velocities are only moderately worse on average and outperform flow initialization on multiple individual scenes. Statistical significance and zero- or constant-velocity baselines are absent.

Several reproducibility-critical details are missing or insufficiently defined, including how dynamic masks are obtained, the voxel-grid resolution and extent, alpha_0, the exact dynamic optimization losses, mask construction for flame-region metrics, and calibration of synchronization accuracy. The paper asserts approximately 15-microsecond precision but provides no direct timing-error measurement.

Only 100 frames at 400 Hz—about 0.25 seconds—are reconstructed from each 15-second recording. All experiments use one three-camera rig and dataset, with no synthetic geometry ground truth, independent capture setup, different camera count, or robustness study for calibration and flow errors. This limits support for the claims of robust reconstruction across real-world fire scenarios.

strengths: The manuscript tackles a genuinely difficult and relevant computer-vision problem: reconstructing fast, transparent, emissive flames from only three consumer cameras. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/7d378f52cb2441b19bc54f52f38af4fe/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The complete capture-and-reconstruction pipeline is practically motivated. Its combination of camera synchronization, static/dynamic decomposition, stereo-monocular background initialization, optical-flow fusion, and temporally parameterized Gaussians produces visually appealing results using relatively inexpensive hardware.

The captured dataset covers 17 scenes and several fuels, backgrounds, flame scales, and wind conditions. Per-scene results are supplied rather than only aggregate metrics, and the authors promise code and full-data release.

The paper includes useful component studies. In particular, separate static-scene pretraining produces a large depth-metric improvement, while flow initialization generally improves flame-region SSIM. Runtime and hardware requirements are also reported.
The presentation is mostly understandable, and the limitations section appropriately identifies failures associated with optical flow, linear trajectories, turbulence, and static/dynamic separation.
weaknesses: I assess this as an Algorithms/General submission because no contribution type is declared. Under that standard, the core algorithmic novelty is limited: most of the pipeline combines existing COLMAP/PatchMatch, Depth Anything V2, MEMFOF, vanilla 3DGS, and FreeTimeGS machinery. The principal new elements appear to be a heuristic flow-fusion initialization and capture/synchronization engineering, but neither is validated strongly enough to establish a substantial algorithmic advance.

The evaluation does not convincingly test the central novel-view reconstruction claim. Every eighth temporal frame is withheld, apparently from the same three camera trajectories used for training. This evaluates temporal interpolation at observed viewpoints, not generalization to unseen viewpoints. Novel-view evidence is relegated to an accompanying video, with no held-out-camera ground truth or quantitative protocol.

There is no reliable evidence that the recovered geometry or motion is correct. The reported depth RMSE uses a monocular Depth Anything prediction as pseudo-ground truth after linear alignment, even though monocular depth is also used to initialize and regularize the proposed reconstruction. This is circular and especially problematic for transparent flames, which the paper itself shows that the monocular estimator does not reconstruct correctly. No multiview depth, tomographic reconstruction, calibrated proxy, or 3D flow measurement is provided.

The baseline comparison is not adequately controlled. The proposed method receives dense stereo/monocular geometry, optical-flow initialization, explicit masks, and separately pretrained static Gaussians, whereas the two generic 4DGS baselines are randomly initialized using hyperparameters from a different scene. One baseline is additionally prevented from following its normal densification once it exceeds one million Gaussians. Consequently, the results do not isolate the proposed representation or optimization from a major difference in initialization and prior information.

Only two generic 4DGS baselines are evaluated. There is no comparison with specialized flame, smoke, fluid, tomography, or physics-informed reconstruction methods discussed in related work, nor with stronger sparse-view dynamic reconstruction alternatives. Even if some require more cameras, comparisons under their intended settings or a clear accuracy-versus-camera-count analysis would help substantiate the claimed advance.

The mathematical basis of the 3D-flow fusion is insufficiently justified. Equation (6), (F-u_i)^T u_i=0, supplies only one scalar constraint per camera for a two-dimensional optical-flow observation and is presented as a projection constraint without derivation. It is unclear why matching only the component along the constructed back-projection vector correctly characterizes all 3D motions consistent with the measured image displacement. Sensitivity to conditioning, camera configuration, regularization alpha_0, and voxel resolution is not studied.

Important implementation details are missing from the manuscript. The source of the dynamic/fire masks used for initialization and masked evaluation is not specified; alpha_0, voxel size, mask construction, dynamic-stage loss, temporal normalization, and several optimization settings are absent or unclear. Releasing code is helpful but does not replace a reproducible method description.

Several highlighted contributions receive little empirical support. Disabling rolling-shutter modeling is numerically indistinguishable and is slightly better on some aggregate metrics. Introducing a full-frame synchronization error causes only a modest change. Random-flow initialization is close in PSNR and LPIPS and outperforms the proposed initialization on several individual scenes. These results weaken claims that microsecond synchronization, rolling-shutter correction, and flow initialization are essential.

Each nominally 15-second capture is evaluated using only 100 frames at 400 Hz—approximately 0.25 seconds. This is a very short interval for testing temporal coherence, changing topology, or sustained turbulent dynamics. There is no long-horizon evaluation, and the linear velocity/lifetime model is therefore tested in a particularly favorable regime.

Photometric metrics are dominated by the static background, while the flame-only masks and their construction are not documented. Results are reported from randomized optimization without repeated runs, confidence intervals over seeds, or significance tests, despite repeated claims of significant improvement.

Claims of “physically plausible” reconstruction, explicit motion analysis, and suitability for downstream tasks such as robot navigation are unsupported. The model uses short-lived Gaussians with linear velocities and image reconstruction losses, without physical constraints or evaluation of recovered trajectories. Overall, the system is promising, but the circular geometry metric, non-novel-view test split, and uncontrolled baselines prevent a convincing scientific case for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a difficult and relatively underexplored computer-vision problem: reconstructing fast, translucent, emissive flames from only three cameras. The decomposition into a depth-regularized static background and flow-initialized dynamic Gaussians is practical and well motivated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/4c6b0a0f356f4efd875f5d58215d786c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The low-cost synchronization apparatus is a clever systems contribution: Gray-code LEDs establish frame correspondence, while rolling-shutter transitions provide approximately 15-microsecond timing precision with consumer cameras.

The evaluation covers 17 real fire scenes with varied fuels, flame scales, wind conditions, smoke, and backgrounds. Per-scene results are supplied, and the qualitative examples show plausible high-frequency flame appearance and substantially cleaner geometry than the tested 4DGS baselines.

Results on dynamic regions are encouraging: the method improves mean flame PSNR from 25.51 to 27.46 and flame SSIM from 0.8019 to 0.8469 relative to the stronger baseline. The large improvement in the reported depth proxy is also consistent with the qualitative depth renderings.

The ablations isolate flow initialization, synchronization, rolling-shutter rendering, and separate static pretraining. It is commendably reported that rolling-shutter modeling provides essentially no measurable aggregate benefit, while static pretraining has a large effect on geometric stability.

The paper is generally clear, discusses meaningful limitations, reports training and rendering costs, and promises both code and the full dataset. At roughly 131 rendered frames per second, the resulting representation may also be useful for downstream visualization or analysis.
weaknesses: The central novel-view claim is not evaluated rigorously. Holding out every eighth frame tests temporal interpolation at the same three camera viewpoints, not spatial generalization to an unseen viewpoint. Novel-view trajectories are assessed only through a supplementary video, without held-out-camera metrics or ground-truth images.

The depth evaluation is not based on measured geometry. RMSE is computed against linearly aligned monocular depth, while monocular depth from Depth Anything V2 is also used to initialize and regularize the proposed reconstruction. This makes the very large depth advantage potentially circular and does not establish metric or even independently validated geometric accuracy.

The baseline study is narrow and asymmetric. Both 4DGS baselines are randomly initialized, whereas the proposed method receives stereo depth, monocular depth, optical flow, segmentation, static-scene pretraining, and calibrated timing. There is no vanilla FreeTimeGS baseline, no comparison using matched auxiliary information, and no comparison to another sparse-view or flow/depth-assisted dynamic reconstruction method. Moreover, Yang et al.'s densification is capped because of memory limits. These choices make it difficult to attribute the gains specifically to the proposed technical ideas.

Several advertised components have limited empirical support. Removing rolling-shutter rendering slightly improves the aggregate flame metrics, synchronization produces only a modest improvement under an artificial offset, and random-flow initialization trails the full model by only 0.45 dB on average despite being presented as a key contribution. Statistical testing or convergence/stability measurements would make these conclusions more convincing.

The 3D-flow formulation needs a clearer derivation. Equation 6 imposes only the scalar condition `(F-u_i)^T u_i=0` per camera; it is not evident that this is equivalent to matching the complete two-dimensional projected flow. A standard projection-Jacobian constraint would normally supply two constraints per view. The paper should justify this equation and analyze failure cases caused by optical-flow errors, occlusion, and view-dependent flame appearance.

Important reproducibility details remain unclear in the manuscript, including how dynamic masks are obtained, voxel-grid resolution and bounds, the value of the flow regularizer, loss terms used during dynamic optimization, Gaussian counts, and the exact construction of flame masks for evaluation. The intended public release helps, but the scientific description should be sufficient on its own.

The method assumes that flames are brighter than the background and that static and dynamic content can be separated cleanly. This may fail for bright backgrounds, strong illumination changes, smoke, reflections, moving surroundings, or fire-background interactions; the current dataset does not systematically quantify these regimes. Overall, the contribution is promising and favors a borderline acceptance, but its strongest geometry and novel-view claims need more independent evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a difficult and practically relevant vision problem: reconstructing transient, semi-transparent, emissive flames from only three cameras. The static/dynamic decomposition is well motivated for this regime.

The proposed pipeline is coherent and practical, combining stereo-monocular background initialization, optical-flow-based dynamic initialization, finite-lifetime moving Gaussians, motion masking, and inexpensive camera synchronization.

Evaluation covers 17 varied real fire sequences and three simulated scenes. Against four dynamic Gaussian-splatting baselines, the method obtains substantial improvements in flame-region PSNR/SSIM, full-frame perceptual metrics, and temporal video quality. The qualitative results also show visibly sharper flames and more stable depth.

The synthetic experiments attempt to evaluate recovered motion rather than relying exclusively on image fidelity. The flow-initialization and masking ablations support their importance for velocity reconstruction.

The manuscript is generally clear, includes useful limitations, reports compute and memory requirements, and provides extensive supplementary implementation and per-scene details. Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, Algorithms/General is appropriate; the capture system and dataset are valuable supporting systems contributions.
weaknesses: The central novel-view reconstruction claim is not adequately validated. Every eighth temporal frame is held out, but all three camera viewpoints appear to be used for training. Thus the quantitative results primarily measure temporal interpolation at observed views. Novel camera trajectories are evaluated only qualitatively, without held-out-camera ground truth or quantitative view extrapolation results.

The claimed real-world depth accuracy is measured against an aligned monocular depth prediction rather than measured depth. Moreover, Depth Anything is already used to initialize and regularize the static reconstruction. RMSE against this proxy therefore demonstrates agreement with a learned prior, not geometric accuracy, and is partially coupled to the pipeline.

The derivation of the fused 3D flow is insufficiently justified and appears questionable. A 2D optical-flow observation ordinarily supplies two constraints through the projection Jacobian, whereas Eq. 4 imposes only the scalar condition `(F-u_i)^T u_i=0`. The paper does not establish that this condition is equivalent to reproducing the measured image flow, particularly under perspective projection.

The proposed DVE protocol evaluates ground-truth velocity only at the locations and with the density weights of predicted Gaussians. It consequently does not clearly penalize missing reconstructed flame volume or biased spatial support. Its robustness to Gaussian scale, opacity, density, and thresholding is not analyzed. Even under this metric, the reported relative L2 error of 0.825 remains large, making the stronger physical-accuracy language premature.

The synchronization contribution receives weak empirical support: NoSync changes real-scene PSNR from 26.93 to 26.89 and leaves several metrics effectively unchanged; the synthetic degradation is also modest. There is no comparison using naturally unsynchronized cameras, multiple offset magnitudes, or the explicit rolling-shutter correction.

The algorithmic novelty is moderate. The temporal Gaussian parameterization is adopted from FreeTimeGS, while the other main elements are established depth, optical-flow, masking, and two-stage reconstruction components. The paper's value therefore depends heavily on strong task-specific validation, for which the missing novel-view and geometric ground truth experiments are important gaps.

The comparison is restricted to Gaussian-splatting methods based on an efficiency argument, but neither training/rendering efficiency comparisons nor representative non-GS volumetric or physics-informed baselines are reported. This weakens broad claims that the approach makes sparse-view fire reconstruction tractable relative to prior work.

Reproducibility is not yet complete: the manuscript promises code and data, but the official repository field is blank, and several important parameters—such as voxel resolution, Tikhonov coefficient, motion-mask construction, lifetime units, and camera geometry—are not fully specified.

strengths: The paper targets a difficult and practically relevant computer-vision problem: reconstructing rapidly varying, semi-transparent flames from only three high-speed camera views.

The static/dynamic decomposition, stereo-plus-monocular background initialization, optical-flow-based volumetric initialization, and transient Gaussian parameterization form a coherent system. The presentation is generally clear, with useful implementation details and qualitative visualizations.

The evaluation covers 17 real captures with varied fuels and backgrounds, alongside three simulated scenes with known velocity fields. Reporting flame-region image metrics, video quality, depth proxies, and motion metrics is broader than relying on full-frame PSNR alone.

The proposed method substantially outperforms the tested dynamic-GS baselines on the reported image metrics, and the synthetic experiments suggest that flow initialization improves directional motion recovery. Training and rendering costs are also practically attractive.

The capture setup and dataset construction are potentially valuable. Asset licensing is reported for the synthetic environments, and the paper acknowledges relevant limitations involving optical flow, linear trajectories, smoke, and background interaction.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess the submission as Algorithms/General. Much of its merit is arguably Applied/Systems: the central representation—Gaussian lifetime, temporal opacity, and constant velocity—is explicitly inherited from FreeTimeGS, while decomposition, monocular-depth regularization, masking, and flow initialization are integrations of established components. Under either framing, the methodological originality is limited relative to the paper's broad claims.

The real-data depth evaluation is circular and cannot establish geometric accuracy. RMSE is measured against linearly aligned Depth Anything predictions, while aligned Depth Anything depth is also used as a strong regularizer in the proposed pipeline. Competing methods do not receive that same prior. Calling this metric flame-depth 'accuracy' or evidence of meaningful 3D structure is therefore unjustified.

The evaluation does not quantitatively test novel viewpoints, despite novel-view synthesis and arbitrary camera trajectories being central claimed capabilities. Every eighth temporal frame is withheld from the same three input cameras, which mainly tests temporal interpolation at observed viewpoints. Novel trajectories are shown only qualitatively and without ground truth; with just three cameras, this is a consequential omission.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently established. Several baselines use their original COLMAP initialization and a configuration for the unrelated DyNeRF 'flame salmon' scene, whereas the proposed system receives specialized background reconstruction, monocular depth, motion masks, synchronization, and flow initialization. A controlled comparison using common background geometry and comparable priors is needed. Excluding non-GS fire or volumetric reconstruction methods solely because they may be slower also prevents evaluation against the most task-relevant literature, and no measured quality-efficiency frontier supports this exclusion.

The proposed DVE motion protocol has important validity problems. It evaluates ground-truth velocity only at each method's predicted Gaussians and weights samples by that method's own scale-volume and opacity, so a reconstruction can avoid penalties in missing or difficult regions. There is no coverage/recall term, no analysis of sensitivity to scale or opacity, and no sufficiently precise explanation of how comparable velocities are extracted from baselines with different temporal parameterizations. Moreover, the method's relative L2 error of 0.825 remains large, weakening the claim of physically accurate recovery.

Several headline components are weakly supported by the ablations. Removing synchronization changes flame PSNR from 26.93 to 26.89 and leaves most real-image metrics essentially unchanged, while even slightly improving full-image PSNR. Removing the mask improves every reported real-image metric and depth proxy. These results may support modest motion-prior effects, but not the claimed necessity of precise custom synchronization or uniformly robust reconstruction.

The experiments use only 100 frames from each 15-second, 400-Hz recording—about 0.25 seconds—making the constant-velocity model and temporal interpolation task substantially easier than reconstructing sustained flame evolution. There is no evaluation over longer durations, different camera counts or baselines, lower frame rates, calibration noise, synchronization errors beyond half a frame, smoke-rich scenes, or backgrounds affected by illumination and combustion.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The supplement omits key values such as voxel resolution/extent, Tikhonov parameter, mask construction, Gaussian counts, and detailed preprocessing. The 'Code and Data' section points to an empty repository location in the submitted PDF. This is especially problematic for a pipeline whose results depend heavily on preprocessing and initialization.

The language overstates physical and volumetric fidelity. The method remains a standard alpha-composited GS appearance model with short-lived linear trajectories; it does not model emission-absorption transport, temperature, density, combustion, or turbulent dynamics. Consequently, claims about photorealistic arbitrary-view fire, explicit physical analysis, and downstream robot navigation go beyond the supplied evidence. Overall, the promising system and dataset do not overcome the circular geometry evaluation, missing novel-view validation, and asymmetric comparisons, so the balance favors rejection.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, this is best assessed as Applied/Systems rather than purely Algorithms/General: its main value is a practical end-to-end system for sparse-view reconstruction of a difficult transient phenomenon. Under that framing, the combination of three-camera high-speed capture, microsecond-scale visual synchronization, static/dynamic decomposition, and efficient Gaussian rendering is useful and sufficiently distinctive.

The transient flame-Gaussian formulation is well motivated. Finite lifetimes, explicit velocities, flow-based volumetric initialization, and separation from the static background directly address the persistence, depth-collapse, and geometric-absorption failure modes identified for conventional dynamic Gaussian methods.

The empirical scope is strong for this specialized problem: 17 real sequences spanning several fuels and flame conditions, three synthetic scenes with ground-truth velocity fields, four relevant Gaussian-splatting baselines, component ablations, per-scene results, and video-level evaluation.

Results consistently favor the proposed system. On real scenes it improves flame PSNR from the best baseline's 24.48 to 26.93 and full-image PSNR from 32.41 to 35.89; on synthetic data it obtains substantially better directional motion agreement, with cosine similarity 0.744 versus at most 0.225 for the baselines.

The paper is clearly organized and visually convincing. It also reports practical efficiency—approximately 30 minutes of training, 8 GB GPU memory, and 131 Hz rendering—and provides unusually concrete capture, synchronization, rolling-shutter, dataset, and hardware details.
The limitations discussion appropriately identifies dependence on optical flow, the restricted constant-velocity model, static/dynamic interaction assumptions, and residual synchronization errors.
weaknesses: The quantitative real-world protocol primarily holds out every eighth frame from the same three captured views. This demonstrates temporal interpolation at observed viewpoints, but does not quantitatively validate the prominent novel-view-synthesis claim; novel camera trajectories are evaluated only qualitatively.

The reported real-world depth metric is not based on measured depth. It compares rendered flame depth to linearly aligned monocular Depth Anything predictions, even though depth for transparent, emissive flames is intrinsically ambiguous. Calling this 'depth accuracy' is therefore too strong, and use of the same depth model elsewhere in the pipeline further weakens its independence as evidence.

The algorithmic novelty is moderate: the temporal Gaussian parameterization is adapted from FreeTimeGS, while several other components are established tools assembled into a specialized pipeline. The paper's acceptance case is consequently stronger as an Applied/Systems contribution than as a broadly novel reconstruction algorithm.

The synchronization ablation shows only negligible real-image changes—26.93 versus 26.89 flame PSNR and identical rounded LPIPS/SSIM—and relatively small synthetic changes. This does not strongly substantiate the claimed importance of the custom synchronization apparatus under the tested motion regime.

Physical validation remains limited to three simulated scenes. The best relative velocity error is still high at 0.825, and no real-world velocity or geometric ground truth is provided, so claims of physically meaningful motion should remain qualified as improved plausibility rather than accurate recovery.

Baseline coverage is restricted to Gaussian-based approaches on efficiency grounds, but training-time and rendering-efficiency comparisons are not actually reported for those baselines. Comparisons to representative neural volumetric or physics-informed fire reconstruction methods would help distinguish gains due to the proposed formulation from a weakness of the selected model family.

Reproducibility is not yet complete: the manuscript promises code and data release, but the repository field in the supplied supplement is blank. Some important choices—voxel resolution, Tikhonov parameter, motion-mask construction, and precise evaluation-mask protocol—also need clearer specification.
